name: Ashpile Stitch-Thermal Underlayer
description: Hand-stitched from salvaged insulation batting, reclaimed synth-fleece strips, and scavenged thermal foil remnants, this underlayer is a patchwork of mismatched gray, rust, and industrial yellow. Every seam is doubled by hand with waxed thread — some sections re-stitched three or four times over. The surface is uneven, lumpy in places, but it holds heat against Shelf cold and acid-rain damp with stubborn efficiency. Worn edges are bound with whatever ribbon or cord was available.
functionality: Passive thermal retention against sub-zero Shelf temperatures and acid-rain moisture; no smart features, no power draw — just layered insulation that works when the grid doesn't.
what_it_says: You make do with what the city throws away, and you've gotten very good at it.
worn_by: kids who inherited their parents' patch jobs
story_hooks: A distinctive patch of orange industrial foil matches a scrap found at a sealed-off collapse site — someone was there when the building came down.
The inner lining contains a hand-sewn pocket with a folded paper note in a language the wearer can't read.
A Shelf kid trades one of these to a Tier 3 journalist who's going undercover — it's the most honest thing they've ever worn.

physical_description.visual_profile: A visibly handmade thermal base layer that reads as utilitarian survival wear. The silhouette is loose and slightly shapeless, prioritizing function over form. Patchwork sections in mismatched grays, rusted oranges, and industrial yellows create an unplanned, almost abstract aesthetic. The overall impression is of something cobbled together from necessity rather than design — authentic sub-grade fabrication.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and oversized through the torso and shoulders, with a slightly tapered waist to prevent bunching under outer layers. Sleeves are long and loose-fitting, ending in bound cuffs of mismatched cord and ribbon.
physical_description.primary_material: Salvaged insulation batting, reclaimed synth-fleece strips, and thermal foil remnants stitched together. Binding edges use whatever scavenged ribbon or paracord was available.
physical_description.texture: Deliberately uneven and lumpy, with visible hand-stitching throughout. Double and triple-stitched seams create raised ridges of waxed thread. The surface has a quilted, padded quality with intentional bulk to trap heat. Edges are deliberately worn and fraying, bound with rough utility cord.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary palette of industrial gray, rust orange, and faded yellow. Sections are arranged in irregular patches with no aesthetic pattern — purely functional placement. Waxed thread seams read as darker, weathered lines across the fabric.
physical_description.closures: None — pulls on over the head. No zippers or fasteners; the garment relies on friction fit and layering.
distinctive_features: Visible hand-stitching with waxed thread throughout
Multiple re-stitched sections showing repair history
Uneven, lumpy insulation padding visible through thin spots
Mismatched binding on sleeve cuffs and neckline using scavenged rope and ribbon
Thermal foil reflective patches visible in places where batting has worn thin
Frayed edges and distressed wear suggesting extended use in harsh conditions
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 — Sub-grade salvage wear. No manufacturing overhead, no brand recognition, purely self-crafted survival gear.
physical_description.cultural_context: Marks the wearer as Shelf-dweller or ungoverned zone resident. The aesthetic communicates acceptance of hardship and self-sufficiency through hand-labor. Wearing this signals either poverty or deliberate rejection of corpo supply chains. Associated with acid-rain communities, cold-storage zones, and off-grid survival networks.
physical_description.condition_typical: Perpetually worn-in and patched. Shows signs of repeated thermal stress and acid-rain exposure. Some seams are visibly re-worked. Thermal foil is peeling or absent in high-friction areas. The garment is never pristine — it's a living, evolving piece of repair work.
